paper_context.research_question: Can neural sequence models, in particular a Grid-RNN-based multi-sequence architecture, learn multi-predicate interaction features from raw word sequences and thereby achieve state-of-the-art Japanese predicate argument structure (PAS) analysis performance without relying on syntactic parser outputs?
contribution_style: incremental improvement on a known task
empirical demonstration that syntactic features can be avoided
main_claims: A single-sequence RNN model that uses only word-sequence-derived features already outperforms prior baselines on the NAIST Text Corpus 1.5 for Japanese PAS.

A multi-sequence Grid-RNN model that connects per-predicate sequences (i.e., models inter-sequence connections) further improves performance, especially for zero (omitted) arguments, compared to the single-sequence variant.
The Grid-RNN-based model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5 without using syntactic information from parsers, thereby reducing error propagation from parser pipelines.
Deeper stacked RNN/Grid layers with residual connections yield better performance, indicating the architecture benefits from depth and residual learning.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Overall F1 on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5 (direct empirical comparison to Ouchi et al. 2015 and other baselines)
Per-argument-type performance (Dep vs Zero) and per-case performance (NOM/ACC/DAT), with emphasis on Zero-argument identification
Ablation / architecture comparisons: single-sequence vs multi-sequence (Grid-RNN) and effect of residual connections and depth
Statistical significance testing of improvements (e.g., bootstrap) and robustness across hyperparameter choices
Analysis of whether the model truly captures multi-predicate interactions (qualitative examples or probing) or whether gains come mainly from greater capacity/context encoding
Resource and reproducibility dimensions: use/no-use of external resources and availability of code/implementation details

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that (1) an RNN-based single-sequence model using only word-sequence-derived features can outperform published baselines on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5; (2) extending this to a Grid-RNN multi-sequence model that connects per-predicate sequences captures multi-predicate interactions and yields further improvements—especially for zero (omitted) arguments; (3) deeper stacked RNN/Grid layers with residual connections improve performance, enabling a state-of-the-art result without syntactic parser inputs. The empirical evidence is test-set F1 comparisons (Table 1, Table 3) and depth/residual narratives (Table 2 summary). The reasoning chain links linguistic motivation (multi-predicate interactions help zero arguments) → architectural design (single-sequence to Grid-RNN multi-sequence + residuals) → empirical gains on NAIST 1.5. Strengths: coherent architectural mapping to the problem, sensible ablation axes (single vs multi, depth, residuals), and use of a standard benchmark. Key breaks or weak links: causal attribution that gains stem from inter-sequence connections (vs capacity/hyperparameter differences) is asserted but not directly tested with capacity-matched baselines or ablations; statistical reporting is limited to a single best-dev-epoch and selective significance markers (no seed variance or full CI); preprocessing choices (use of corpus-provided tokenization and gold predicate positions) complicate the claim of 'no external resources' or real-world pipeline robustness. I flag novelty as plausible (Grid-RNN applied to multi-predicate PAS) but risky because prior joint models did use multi-predicate signals albeit via syntactic features; the manuscript does not provide probing evidence that multi-predicate interactions are used in specific cases beyond aggregate F1 improvements. Recommended verification steps are capacity-controlled baselines, ablation of inter-sequence links, seed-averaged results, and qualitative probing/visualization to strengthen causal claims.
logical_argument_graph: Motivation: Zero (omitted) arguments in pro-drop languages are hard because they lack syntactic dependencies; multi-predicate interactions and sentence-wide context are linguistic cues that can help (Sec. 2, 2.2).

Design Step 1 (Single-Sequence): Use stacked Bi-RNNs over candidate argument sequences with word/predicate/mark embeddings to induce sentence-level context-sensitive features and predict per-word labels via softmax (Sec. 3).

Design Step 2 (Multi-Sequence Grid-RNN): Create M sequences—one per predicate—and use Grid-RNN inter-sequence concatenations to allow information flow across predicates, aiming to model multi-predicate interactions directly from word sequences (Sec. 4.1–4.2).
Optimization/Capacity: Add depth and residual connections to enable training of deeper RNN/Grid stacks, hypothesizing improved representation learning with depth (Sec. 4.2).

Empirical Test: Evaluate Single-Seq and Multi-Seq models (with up to 8 layers) on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5; compare to published baselines (Imamura+09 reimpl., Ouchi+15) using F1 measures and bootstrap significance (Sec. 6, Tables 1 & 3).
Observed Result A: Single-Seq outperforms prior baselines on All/Zero/Dep metrics, implying word-sequence-only features suffice to improve over parser-reliant systems (Table 1).

Observed Result B: Multi-Seq (Grid-RNN) further improves over Single-Seq (modest absolute gains, notably ~1.0 F1 on Zero), suggesting inter-sequence connections capture beneficial multi-predicate interactions (Table 1, Sec. 6).

Observed Result C: Deeper models with residual connections yield additional gains (~1.0 F1 when using 8 layers with residuals versus without), implying depth + residuals ease optimization and improve performance (Table 2 narrative).

Conclusion: The Grid-RNN multi-sequence architecture enables state-of-the-art PAS analysis on NAIST 1.5 without external syntactic features and particularly helps zero-argument identification (Conclusion).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes neural sequence models for Japanese PAS analysis: a single-sequence stacked Bi-RNN (GRU) model that uses only word-sequence-derived features, and a multi-sequence Grid-RNN model that connects per-predicate sequences to model multi-predicate interactions. Experiments on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5 show that both models outperform prior baselines (Imamura et al. 2009 reimplementation and Ouchi et al. 2015 joint model) with modest absolute gains overall and larger relative gains on zero (omitted) arguments. Residual connections and increased depth reportedly improve performance. Key claims are that (i) syntactic parser outputs are not required to reach state-of-the-art on NAIST 1.5, (ii) Grid-RNN inter-sequence connections capture multi-predicate interactions and help zero-argument identification, and (iii) residual/deeper RNN/Grid stacks aid learning. For these results to hold, several methodological conditions must be true (e.g., fair baseline parity, control for model capacity, robust statistical testing, reproducible preprocessing). The manuscript provides useful implementation details (Theano, hyperparameter ranges, dev-model selection) and publicly available code link, but it lacks several robustness checks: seed-averaged results, capacity-matched baselines, targeted ablations isolating inter-sequence links, and direct probing that the Grid-RNN uses multi-predicate information rather than increased parameterization or lexical/contextual cues. Comparisons rely on published baseline numbers or reimplementations (Ouchi et al. 2015), and significance is reported only via bootstrap for some comparisons without full reporting of the test configuration (number of resamples, exact p-values, or confidence intervals). Several assumptions are explicit (use of annotated tokenization/predicates, selection by best-dev-epoch), and they introduce risks to claimed generality. I list concrete strengths, concerns, comparable works, alternative interpretations, and recommended experiments for stronger causal attribution and reproducibility.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that multi-predicate interactions, important for Japanese PAS and especially zero-argument resolution, can be learned directly from raw word sequences via neural sequence models. Starting from a single-sequence stacked Bi-RNN that builds context-sensitive word/argument candidate encodings and predicts case labels with per-word softmax, the authors extend to a multi-sequence Grid-RNN that connects per-predicate sequences so information propagates across predicates. They add residual connections to ease optimization of deeper stacks. Empirically on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5, both models exceed prior baselines, and the Grid-RNN variant yields modest but statistically signficant gains overall and for zero arguments. The paper's reasoning chain: (i) multi-predicate interactions matter; (ii) Grid-RNNs are an architectural mechanism to encode such interactions without external syntactic parses; (iii) deeper networks with residuals better capture context; (iv) measured gains on NAIST 1.5 validate the approach and its practical value of avoiding parser error propagation. However, attribution of gains to inter-sequence modeling (vs capacity/hyperparameters) and the external-validity of 'no-syntax' claims need further control and probing evidence.

Architectural extension: Introduce Grid-RNN to connect per-predicate sequences (inter-sequence edges) to model multi-predicate interactions jointly.
Optimization improvement: Add residual connections and increase depth to improve representational capacity and trainability.

Interpretation: Grid-RNNs capture multi-predicate interactions and sentence-level context sufficiently to match/exceed prior parser-dependent systems.
Caveat: Alternative explanations (parameter count, selection bias, preprocessing, lack of probing) could account for some gains; further experiments needed to isolate mechanism.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: Reconstructed reasoning: The paper argues that (1) contextualized sequence encodings from stacked Bi-RNNs can replace syntactic parser features for Japanese PAS, producing a competitive single-sequence model; (2) explicitly connecting predicate-specific sequences via a Grid-RNN (multi-sequence model) allows propagation of inter-predicate signals across predicates in a sentence, and therefore yields further gains, especially for zero (omitted) arguments; (3) deeper stacked RNN/Grid layers with residual connections enable better optimization and improve performance; (4) when trained and evaluated on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5 (using corpus-provided tokenization and predicate targets), these models exceed previously reported baselines (notably Ouchi et al. 2015) without relying on external syntactic parsers. Evidence comes from test-set F1 numbers (Table 1: Single-Seq 81.15, Multi-Seq 81.42 vs Ouchi+15 79.23), per-type breakdowns showing larger relative gains on Zero arguments, and narrative/ablation-style reporting about depth/residuals (Table 2 summary). The paper's causal chain assumes that inter-sequence concatenation in Grid-RNNs transmits predicate-level clues that disambiguate omitted arguments; residuals ease optimization of deep stacks; and sequence-only features suffice when the model sees all predicates jointly. Gaps in the chain: capacity controls (parameter-count matched baselines) and explicit probing of whether inter-predicate signal, rather than extra parameters or implicit lexical/contextual cues, drive the gains are missing. Statistical reporting uses bootstrap resampling for some comparisons, but the experimental stability across multiple seeds, and exact settings for significance tests, are incomplete. The “no syntactic information” claim is credible in the sense that no external parser outputs were used, but the model relies on gold word boundaries and target predicate annotations from NAIST, which narrows external-dependency-free claims in realistic pipelines.

Empirical results on NAIST 1.5 (Single-Seq and Multi-Seq) -> numeric improvement over Ouchi+2015 -> claim: state-of-the-art without syntactic parser features

The paper's reasoning links linguistic motivation (multi-predicate interactions aid zero resolution) to the Grid-RNN design and to empirical gains. Evidence in the manuscript (Tables, architecture descriptions) supports most empirical claims about observed numeric improvements. However, causal attribution that gains arise specifically from inter-sequence interaction modeling (rather than capacity/hyperparameter differences), and generalization claims about doing well “without syntactic information” in realistic pipelines, are only partially supported by the presented experiments. Statistical reporting and robustness checks (seed averages, capacity-matched baselines, targeted ablations/probing) are limited or absent, introducing uncertainty around effect size significance and mechanism. I therefore parse claims as: supported (empirical improvement observed on NAIST 1.5), partially supported (Grid-RNN improves Zero arguments but causality unclear), and potentially overstated (claims that the model captures multi-predicate interactions in a mechanistic sense and that syntactic parsers are unnecessary in practice) until additional controlled analyses are shown.

concerns.description: The multi-sequence Grid-RNN uses larger GRU input parameters (multi-sequence GRU input dims 64×32 vs single-sequence 32×32), so observed gains may be due to increased parameter count/capacity rather than the inter-sequence topology itself.

concerns.title: Limited statistical robustness reporting
concerns.description: Results are reported for the single epoch with best development F1; no seed-averaged metrics, standard deviations, or full bootstrap configuration (resamples, paired testing) provided for key comparisons.

Table 1 marks significance by bootstrap but does not provide resample counts or p-values.

Shared Analysis recommendation list suggests ablations and probing.

evidence: Text: 'performance tends to get better as the RNN or Grid layers get deeper with residual connections' and 'two models with 8 layers and residual connections achieved considerable improvements of around 1.0 point'.
Full per-depth numeric table (Table 2) not included in excerpt.

uncertainty_flags: Key numeric gains (≈0.27 overall F1; ≈1.0 F1 on Zero) are modest — their robustness depends on multiple-run variance and bootstrap test specifics not fully reported.
Parameterization differences between Single-Seq and Multi-Seq raise capacity-confound concerns (GRU sizes differ).
Use of gold tokenization and predicate annotations may inflate results relative to pipeline use; 'no external resources' should be clarified.
Causal claim that Grid-RNN 'captures multi-predicate interactions' is not supported by direct probing or ablation isolating inter-sequence signaling.
alternative_interpretations: Gains from Multi-Seq arise mainly from larger parameter count or different GRU dimensions rather than the grid topology conveying inter-predicate information.

Zero-class improvements could stem from modeling richer lexical/contextual co-occurrences across the sentence (e.g., selectional preferences) available in sequence encodings, not specifically predicate-to-predicate message passing.
Residual/depth improvements might reflect better optimization due to different hyperparameter choices or regularization at deeper sizes rather than novel representational power.
transparency_notes: Authors provide many hyperparameter ranges and training details but report single best-dev-epoch results; seed-averaged runs and exact bootstrap test parameters should be added.
Code availability is mentioned ('publicly available at http:xxx') but no permanent link or exact commit/version is cited in the excerpt.
Dataset split follows standard NAIST 1.5 partitions; explicit mention that gold predicates and tokenization were used should be maintained and discussed as a limitation for pipeline scenarios.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Applying Grid-style recurrence to predicate sequences for PAS is a meaningful architectural adaptation (novelty signal) but novelty alone does not establish that the inter-sequence mechanism, rather than capacity, produces the empirical gains; additional controlled analyses are required to separate novelty from explanatory validity.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If capacity-matched single-sequence baselines still underperform Multi-Seq, then grid inter-sequence topology likely drives gains.
If masking other predicates or randomizing predicate order reduces Multi-Seq performance substantially more than Single-Seq, it would support that inter-predicate interactions are being exploited.
If Multi-Seq maintains gains when trained with automatic tokenization and predicate detection (non-gold preprocessing), claim of parser-independence becomes stronger.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Grid-RNN application to per-predicate multi-sequence modeling for PAS is an adaptive reuse of known grid recurrence ideas applied to a new dimension (predicates). It extends existing neural PAS work that used sentence-level RNNs by adding explicit inter-predicate connections.
evidence: Manuscript Sec.4 describes inter-sequence concatenation in Grid layers.
Related work cites Kalchbrenner et al. (2016) and prior PAS neural papers (Iida et al., Shibata et al.).
uncertainty_flags: Risk that practical novelty is smaller if gains are due to capacity rather than topology.

novelty_lenses.verdict: moderate empirical impact conditional on robustness
novelty_lenses.rationale: Reported improvements on NAIST 1.5 and better Zero resolution are valuable for the PAS community, but the impact depends on reproducibility, statistical stability, and pipeline robustness (gold preprocessing).
evidence: Table 1/3 show performance improvements over Ouchi+15, especially on Zero and some case roles.
uncertainty_flags: Magnitude of gains modest; lacking seed-averages and pipeline robustness tests.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The architecture is designed to propagate information across predicates, a plausible mechanism, but the manuscript doesn't present direct evidence (ablation/probing) that the mechanism is responsible for the observed improvements.
evidence: Grid-RNN inter-sequence concatenation design (Sec.4.2).
Improved Zero F1 in Multi-Seq vs Single-Seq.
uncertainty_flags: No targeted probes, example-based analyses, or capacity-controlled ablations provided.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident (45–90%) in the core empirical observation that the proposed Grid-RNN model reports higher test F1 on NAIST 1.5 than the cited baselines (given the clear numeric table). The wide interval reflects uncertainty from single-run reporting, capacity confounds, and missing ablations/probing that would be needed to firmly support causal and generalization claims.

consensus_findings: The paper presents a coherent architectural proposal: stacked Bi-RNN encoders (single-sequence) extended to a Grid-RNN multi-sequence formulation that explicitly connects per-predicate sequences; residual connections are used to train deeper stacks.

Reported empirical results on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5 show that both the single-sequence and multi-sequence models achieve higher test-set F1 than the cited baselines, with especially larger relative gains on the Zero (omitted-argument) category.

Reviewers agree that evaluating on NAIST 1.5 is appropriate and that the task motivation (multi-predicate interactions aiding zero-argument resolution) is linguistically plausible and matches the architectural choices.
There is broad agreement that the manuscript includes useful implementation detail and that public code availability (as claimed) would materially aid reproducibility.

There is unanimous concern that key methodological controls and reporting are missing or incomplete: seed-averaged metrics / run variance, capacity-matched baselines, targeted ablations of inter-sequence links, and detailed description of statistical tests.
disagreements: Degree of novelty: some reviewers consider the Grid-RNN application to predicate×token axes a moderately novel and meaningful adaptation of prior Grid/MD-RNN work; others view it as incremental (composing known elements) — the disagreement centers on whether application to PAS is a significant architectural advance or an expected extension.

Practical significance of the Multi-Seq improvements: some reviewers emphasize the statistical significance reported (bootstrap) and see the ~1.0 F1 Zero improvement as meaningful for PAS, while others view the absolute magnitude as modest and liable to be explained by variance or capacity differences.

Interpretation of depth/residuals benefits: reviewers differ on how confidently to ascribe gains to residual-enabled depth versus parameter count and optimization/hyperparameter tuning; some accept residuals as the likely optimizer benefit, while others request explicit capacity controls to separate effects.
uncertainty_hotspots: Capacity confound: Multi-Seq and Single-Seq models used different GRU dimensionalizations (multi-seq has larger input-related GRU sizes). Without capacity-matched single-sequence baselines, it is uncertain whether gains stem from inter-sequence topology or simply from more parameters.

Statistical robustness: reported numbers are single best-dev-epoch results with selective bootstrap marking. The absence of averages over multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, and exact bootstrap configuration leaves the reliability of small absolute differences uncertain.

Mechanistic evidence that inter-sequence links are used: there is no targeted probing (ablation of inter-sequence inputs, masking experiments, example-level diagnostics, or representation probes) to demonstrate that Grid-RNN predictions rely on other predicates' information rather than global sentence-level context or lexical cues.

Preprocessing realism: authors used NAIST-provided annotated word boundaries and gold target predicate lists. It is unclear how results transfer to pipeline settings with automatic tokenization and predicate detection, which affects the practical interpretation of 'no external resources' and 'parser-free' claims.

Depth effect attribution: reported improvement with deeper stacks and residuals lacks full per-depth numeric tables and capacity controls, so whether depth or other confounds drive the gains is unsettled.
model_diversity_effects: Single-Sequence effect: moving from parser-based baselines to a sequence-only stacked Bi-RNN appears to produce the largest single-step empirical improvement reported (substantial gain over Ouchi+2015), suggesting that sentence-level contextual encoders alone capture many useful signals for PAS.

Multi-Sequence (Grid-RNN) marginal effect: adding inter-sequence connectivity yields a modest additional improvement overall and a clearer improvement on the Zero class; this indicates potential role-specific benefits (better handling of omitted arguments) but the effect size is small and sensitive to the capacity/statistics confounds.

Depth/residuals effect: deeper stacked layers with residual connections consistently improved results in the reported experiments, implying optimization and representational benefits of depth; however, this effect interacts with model capacity and training stability and thus may vary across architectures and hyperparameter regimes.

Role-specific sensitivity: gains are concentrated on Zero (omitted) arguments and less pronounced for Dep (dependency) cases and some case labels (NOM/ACC/DAT vary), implying the Grid-RNN or depth helps where long-range and multi-predicate signals matter most; confirmatory probing is needed to assert causality.
meta_review.editor_guidance: As the central decision authority, consider requesting a focused revision that addresses the principal methodological gaps before downstream acceptance actions. Requested revisions should include (1) capacity-controlled experiments: a single-sequence baseline with matched total parameter count to the Multi-Seq model and a Multi-Seq ablation with inter-sequence links disabled (parameter-matched), (2) robustness: report mean and standard deviation across multiple independent runs (e.g., 5–10 seeds) and provide confidence intervals and full bootstrap test settings (number of resamples, paired testing), (3) mechanistic probes: ablation/masking experiments and a small set of qualitative examples showing cases where Multi-Seq changes a Zero prediction and why, (4) preprocessing clarification: explicitly state what 'no external resources' includes/excludes and provide at least one experiment using automatic tokenization and/or predicate detection (or a discussion bounding likely effects), and (5) complete reporting: include the full per-depth numeric table (Table 2) with parameter counts per variant and exact hyperparameter choices. Ask the authors to update the public code repository with exact experiment scripts and random seeds. These targeted additions will materially reduce the principal epistemic uncertainties reviewers raised and enable fair verification.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and enable reproducibility, please perform and report the following concrete actions: (1) Add capacity-matched controls: increase single-sequence model size to match Multi-Seq parameter count and/or reduce Multi-Seq parameters while preserving inter-sequence links, then report comparative results; (2) Ablate inter-sequence links: train a Multi-Seq variant with those concatenations removed or randomized (parameter-matched) to directly test the inter-sequence mechanism; (3) Provide seed-averaged metrics: run each key configuration with multiple random seeds (suggest 5 or more), report mean ± std and 95% CI, and provide full bootstrap test details (resample count, paired/unpaired); (4) Probing and examples: include qualitative case studies where Multi-Seq succeeds and Single-Seq fails for Zero arguments, and run masking/perturbation analyses or simple representation probes that show cross-predicate information is encoded and used; (5) Clarify preprocessing: explicitly state that NAIST gold tokenization and target predicate annotations were used, distinguish these from 'external resources', and, if feasible, include an experiment with automatic tokenization or predicate detection to assess pipeline robustness; (6) Publish code and exact experiment scripts (commit hash) including data split scripts, preprocessing steps, hyperparameters, and random seeds so reviewers and readers can reproduce results; (7) Add the full numeric breakdown for depth/residual experiments (Table 2) including parameter counts per model. Make any claim language about 'without syntactic information' precise and bounded by the preprocessing choices.
transparency_report: Provided by authors: clear architectural descriptions (equations and layer designs), task motivation, experimental dataset (NAIST 1.5), implementation details (framework, optimizer, epoch counts, hyperparameter search ranges), and numerical test-set F1 tables comparing to prior baselines. Authors also state code will be publicly available.

Missing or partial in the manuscript: per-variant parameter counts (full model sizes), per-depth numeric table (Table 2) details in the excerpt, multiple-run (seed) statistics, full bootstrap testing configuration (number of resamples and pairing), capacity-matched baselines and explicit ablation experiments isolating inter-sequence links, and experiments demonstrating robustness to non-gold preprocessing.

Public code note: authors claim a public repository but the URL in the provided excerpts is a placeholder. A working repository with scripts, exact seeds, and data-preprocessing steps is required for full transparency.
epistemic_limits: This synthesis is constrained by the provided manuscript excerpts and reviewers' analyses rather than direct re-execution of experiments or inspection of the authors' code/data. Reviewers did not have access to the claimed public repository (URL redacted in excerpts) or raw training logs; therefore, some assessments (particularly around baseline parity, exact parameter counts, and statistical variance) are inferential. The reviewers' judgments depend on how faithfully published baseline numbers and reimplementations match the authors' preprocessing and split decisions; we cannot confirm that parity. Finally, absence of targeted ablation/probing in the manuscript prevents definitive attribution of mechanism (inter-sequence Grid connections) versus alternative explanations (increased capacity, lexical/contextual modeling), so causal claims remain provisional until controlled experiments are performed.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes using stacked Bi-RNNs (single-sequence) and a Grid-RNN multi-sequence extension to model Japanese predicate argument structure (PAS) from raw word sequences without syntactic parser outputs. On NAIST Text Corpus 1.5 the reported single-sequence model already outperforms cited baselines and the Grid-RNN yields modest additional gains, particularly for zero (omitted) arguments. Deeper stacks with residual connections are claimed to further improve results. Reviewers find the architecture and motivation coherent and the empirical results promising, but identify important methodological and reporting gaps that limit causal attribution and generalization.
strengths: Architectural clarity: explicit mapping from linguistic motivation (multi-predicate interactions, long-range context) to the Grid-RNN multi-sequence design and residual-enabled depth.

Empirical gains on a standard benchmark: reported test-set F1 on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5 shows Single-Seq and Multi-Seq exceed the cited Ouchi et al. (2015) baseline, with larger relative improvement on the Zero class.
Explored ablation axes: paper compares single-sequence vs multi-sequence, and reports effects of depth and residual connections.
Reproducibility intent: implementation details provided (framework, optimizer, hyperparameter ranges) and authors state code will be publicly available.
limitations: Capacity confound between Single-Seq and Multi-Seq: GRU dimensional choices differ (multi-seq uses larger input-related GRU sizes). No capacity-matched single-sequence baseline or parameter-matched ablation is presented, so it is unclear whether Multi-Seq gains stem from inter-sequence connectivity or increased parameterization.

Insufficient statistical robustness reporting: results are reported for the single best-dev-epoch with only selective bootstrap significance notes. No seed-averaged means ± std, confidence intervals for main results, or full bootstrap configuration (resample count, paired/unpaired test) are provided.

Lack of mechanistic/probing evidence: no ablation that disables inter-sequence links, no masking/perturbation experiments, and no qualitative case studies linking improved Zero predictions to information flow from other predicates.

Preprocessing realism not fully addressed: experiments use NAIST-provided annotated word boundaries and gold target predicate annotations; the claim of performing 'without syntactic information' needs qualification and experiments with automatic tokenization/predicate detection are absent.
open_questions: Please provide capacity-controlled comparisons: can the authors report a single-sequence model scaled to match the Multi-Seq total parameter count (or a Multi-Seq variant with matched parameter counts but inter-sequence links removed)?

Please report experimental variance: for key configurations (Single-Seq, Multi-Seq, depth variants) provide results averaged over multiple random seeds (suggest ≥5), with standard deviations and 95% confidence intervals, and state exact bootstrap test settings (number of resamples and whether tests are paired).

Can the authors include targeted ablations/probing that demonstrate Grid-RNN uses other-predicate information (e.g., mask neighboring-predicate inputs, randomize predicate order, or present examples where Multi-Seq corrects Single-Seq because of another predicate)?

Please clarify preprocessing and the scope of 'no external resources': explicitly state that NAIST gold tokenization and gold predicate targets were used, and (ideally) report one experiment using automatic tokenization and/or automatic predicate detection to measure pipeline robustness.
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers agree the architectural idea (Grid-RNN across predicate×token axes) is coherent and plausibly addresses multi-predicate interactions relevant to zero-argument resolution.
All reviewers observe that reported F1 numbers on NAIST 1.5 indicate empirical improvement over the cited baselines, especially for Zero arguments.
All reviewers request stronger methodological controls (capacity-matched baselines, multi-seed reporting) and direct probes/ablations to support causal attribution to the Grid-RNN mechanism.
All reviewers note the need for clarity about preprocessing (gold tokenization and predicate annotations) and for making the claimed public code and experiment scripts available.
disagreement_snapshot: Magnitude and significance interpretation: some reviewers view the ~1.0 F1 Zero-class gain and modest overall gain as practically meaningful (especially given the hard Zero class), while others view these deltas as modest and potentially explainable by capacity or variance without stronger statistical evidence or ablations.

Novelty framing: reviewers diverge on whether applying Grid-style recurrence to predicate-specific sequences is a moderately novel, valuable adaptation versus an incremental combination of known components; this disagreement affects how strongly the architecture's contribution is characterized.

Depth/residual attribution: reviewers differ on confidence that residual connections + depth are the principal cause of reported improvements vs other confounding factors (parameter count, optimization/hyperparameter tuning).
uncertainty_snapshot: Primary uncertainty: whether the Multi-Seq architecture's inter-sequence connectivity causally drives the Zero-class improvements or whether increased capacity/hyperparameter differences explain the gains.
Secondary uncertainty: stability of reported gains across random seeds and whether small reported differences remain significant under repeated runs and full statistical reporting.
Tertiary uncertainty: generalization to realistic pipelines that do not provide gold tokenization or gold predicate lists—i.e., whether the parser-free claim holds under automatic preprocessing.

Reviewer methodological recommendations and statistical norms: request for seed-averaged reporting, capacity-matched baselines, ablation/probing experiments, and explicit bootstrap test configurations (derived from shared reviewer analyses).

Missing: exact public code URL/commit (placeholder in excerpt), per-variant parameter counts, full numeric table for depth experiments (Table 2) in the provided excerpts, multiple-seed averages and standard deviations, and exact bootstrap testing parameters. Authors are encouraged to release experiment scripts, seed logs, preprocessing code (tokenization/predicate extraction), and model checkpoints to enable replication.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request a targeted revision addressing the main methodological gaps before proceeding: (1) add capacity-controlled experiments (parameter-matched single-sequence and/or ablated Multi-Seq without inter-sequence links), (2) report mean ± std over multiple independent random seeds for all key configurations and include 95% CIs and exact bootstrap parameters, (3) include probing/ablation evidence showing that inter-sequence links materially affect Zero predictions (masking, randomization, or qualitative case studies), (4) clarify preprocessing (explicitly state use of NAIST gold tokenization and gold predicate lists) and provide at least one experiment measuring robustness to automatic preprocessing or qualify claims accordingly, and (5) publish the exact code commit, scripts, and seeds. These changes will materially reduce the central epistemic uncertainties reviewers raised.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen empirical and causal claims, please perform and report the following: (a) Capacity controls: train and report a single-sequence model scaled to match Multi-Seq parameter count (or reduce Multi-Seq parameters) and/or present a Multi-Seq variant with inter-sequence concatenations disabled but with matched parameters. (b) Statistical robustness: run each primary configuration with multiple random seeds (recommend ≥5), report mean ± std and 95% CIs, and provide exact bootstrap settings (resample count, paired/unpaired). (c) Mechanistic probes: include ablation/masking experiments (e.g., mask other-predicate sequences at test time, randomize predicate order), targeted qualitative examples where Multi-Seq corrects Single-Seq on Zero cases, and simple representational probes or attribution analyses demonstrating cross-predicate influence. (d) Preprocessing clarity and pipeline robustness: explicitly state what 'no external resources' covers (dataset-provided annotations vs external tools), and if feasible run at least one experiment with automatic tokenization and predicate detection (or discuss expected impact). (e) Complete reporting and artifacts: include full per-depth numeric tables with parameter counts (Table 2), exact hyperparameter choices, training/validation loss curves, and publish the full code repository with scripts, data-split utilities, and seeds/commit hashes to enable reproducibility.
human_facing_meta_review.comments: Summary: The paper proposes stacked Bi-RNNs and a Grid-RNN multi-sequence architecture to learn multi-predicate interaction features from raw word sequences for Japanese PAS. Experiments on NAIST Text Corpus 1.5 report that a single-sequence model outperforms cited baselines and the Grid-RNN adds modest gains, especially for zero (omitted) arguments; deeper residual stacks reportedly improve performance further. Strengths: (1) coherent mapping from linguistic need to architecture and clear Grid-RNN formalization; (2) empirical improvements on a standard benchmark with emphasis on the challenging Zero class; (3) exploration of key axes (single vs multi, depth/residuals) and intention to release code. Limitations: (1) capacity confound between Single-Seq and Multi-Seq models due to differing GRU dimensions—authors should present capacity-matched baselines or parameter-matched ablations; (2) insufficient statistical reporting—results reported as single best-dev-epoch without seed-averaged means, standard deviations, or fully-specified bootstrap tests; (3) absence of mechanistic evidence that Grid-RNN exploits inter-predicate signals (no masking/randomization/ablation or case studies); (4) preprocessing caveat—use of NAIST gold tokenization and gold predicate annotations complicates the practical 'no external resources' / parser-free claim. Open Questions: (1) Can the authors provide parameter-matched single-sequence baselines and/or a Multi-Seq with inter-sequence links disabled to isolate topology effects? (2) Can the authors provide multi-seed averages ± std and 95% CIs and exact bootstrap test configurations for the significance claims? (3) Can the authors add probing and qualitative examples demonstrating that Multi-Seq uses other predicates' information to resolve Zero arguments (e.g., masking experiments, activation/attribution traces)? (4) Please clarify preprocessing: explicitly detail tokenization and predicate extraction steps and, if feasible, show robustness under automatic tokenization/predicate detection. Transparency: good model-level detail and hyperparameter ranges, but missing exact code/commit, per-model parameter counts, per-depth numeric table, seed logs, and full bootstrap settings. Confidence interval: {"lower": 0.45, "upper": 0.85, "rationale": "Moderate confidence that the manuscript presents a coherent architectural idea and that reported numeric improvements on NAIST 1.5 are real in the experimental setting shown; lower bound reflects missing capacity controls, single-run reporting, and absent probing which limit confidence in causal attribution and generalization to pipeline settings." }

confidence_interval.rationale: Moderate confidence: reviewers consistently observe a coherent architecture and measurable gains on NAIST 1.5, but missing capacity-controlled experiments, seed-averaged statistics, and probing/ablation leave causal and generalization claims provisional. The interval reflects confidence in the empirical observation within the provided experimental context but reduced confidence in broader causal and deployment claims until requested controls are supplied.

E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
